Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Vignette:
# Anahera's Vigil

Anahera still remembers the moment she first noticed him—a man in a grey hoodie at the farmer's market on a Saturday morning in late March. She was selecting tomatoes, and when she turned, he was there, thirty feet back, not looking at anything in particular. She thought nothing of it then. By the following Tuesday, when she saw the same hoodie outside the coffee shop where she bought her morning chai, the coincidence began to feel different. By Friday, when he appeared across the street from her apartment building, she knew.

What followed was eight weeks of escalating contact. Messages from unknown numbers. Photos of her arriving at school. A note tucked under her windshield wiper with her address written in capital letters. The police took a report, but the evidence felt scattered—fragmented the way her own memories of those weeks now are. She can recall with crystalline precision the weight of her phone in her pocket, the specific shade of grey of that hoodie, the exact angle of his jaw when he turned to look at her outside the grocery store. But the timeline blurs. She cannot reliably say whether the messages came before or after the photographs, or how many times she actually saw him in person versus how many times she was certain she saw him and later realized she was mistaken. Some days feel completely absent from her recollection, as though those eight weeks have been cut into pieces and some pieces lost entirely.

The stalking stopped abruptly when he was arrested following a traffic stop that revealed outstanding warrants. He was incarcerated on unrelated charges. Anahera's case was dropped. He is still in custody, scheduled for release in fourteen months. She knows this because she checks the inmate database every morning before work, along with the county court records, along with the police report she filed, reading them as though the details might have changed overnight, as though the information might suddenly reveal something that would make sense of what happened to her.

Now, nine months later, Anahera has become someone she does not quite recognize. In her classroom at Lincoln Heights Elementary, where she has taught for three years, she finds herself constantly aware of the position of the door, the location of windows, the proximity of other adults who might intervene if something happened. She teaches a class of eighteen students with significant behavioral and learning disabilities, children who need her presence, her calm, her attention. But Anahera's attention is divided. While a student named Marcus practices reading at the table beside her, part of her is listening to the hallway, tracking the footsteps that pass her classroom door. When footsteps pause outside, her body goes rigid. Her supervisor has begun to notice. Last month, she forgot to submit her weekly progress reports because she spent three hours reviewing security camera footage from the parking lot, looking for a grey hoodie. The week before that, a parent complained that Anahera had seemed distant and distracted during a conference about her son's IEP goals.

At home, she no longer sits on her couch to read or watch television. Sitting still feels dangerous, as though relaxation is a luxury that requires her to lower her guard, and lowering her guard is how people get hurt. She moves through her apartment in patterns, checking the locks on windows and doors multiple times per evening. Her partner, Kai, has grown frustrated and frightened by turns—frustrated at the repetition, frightened by what it suggests about Anahera's state of mind. They argue about whether the locks were already checked, whether the curtains are closed far enough, whether Anahera should go to the grocery store or whether that is too much risk. Kai suggested therapy weeks ago. Anahera resisted, certain that talking about it would only make it more real, would only give it more power. But last week, she found herself unable to teach for three consecutive days, calling in sick while she lay in bed and reviewed the events of the stalking over and over, searching for the moment she should have done something differently, the instant where she might have prevented all of this if she had only been more careful, more aware, more something.

She is calling a therapist today because she is afraid of what will happen if she does not, and equally afraid of what will happen if she does. What terrifies her most is the possibility that even therapy cannot make her feel safe again—that she will remain like this, forever scanning, forever incomplete, forever haunted by the pieces of a story she cannot quite assemble.
